summary: This informational document defines a mechanism for reoptimizing loosely routed MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineered LSPs signaled with RSVP-TE. A head-end can trigger path re-evaluation, and a mid-point can tell it a better path exists or that reoptimization is needed, for example for maintenance. It covers intra- and inter-domain cases.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4736 describes how routers can discover that a loosely routed traffic-engineered path has a better route available, or needs to move for maintenance. Intermediate routers can report this to the path's starting router, which decides whether to reroute it.

questions: how to find better mpls paths
subtitle: How RSVP-TE paths can be rechecked when downstream routes change.

tldr.problem: A loosely routed traffic-engineered path leaves some hops for intermediate routers to calculate. A head-end may not see a lower-cost path that later becomes available in another area or domain.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4736 lets a head-end request path re-evaluation and lets an intermediate router notify it when a better path or maintenance reroute is needed. The head-end decides whether to replace the path.
tldr.outcome: The optional signaling extensions apply to loosely routed MPLS and GMPLS paths signaled with RSVP-TE, within or across routing domains.

today: RFC 4736 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Problem with Loose Hops
sections.content:
A loosely routed label-switched path does not name every router when the head-end signals it. Its route may be absent, may contain a loose hop, or may name an abstract node representing more than one router. Intermediate routers calculate the segment to the next loose hop.

This lets a path cross routing areas or autonomous systems whose details are not visible at the head-end. If a lower-cost path appears later in a downstream area, the head-end may not know about it and cannot choose it without a notification mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting router can name landmarks and let intermediate routers choose the route between them. A later change in a downstream area may create a better route that the starting router cannot see.

sections.title: Re-evaluating an Established Path
sections.content:
RFC 4736 defines two ways to trigger a new path evaluation. The head-end can request that intermediate routers check routes to their next loose or abstract hop. Or a midpoint router can perform its own check after a timer, a network event, or an operator request.

A better path means a lower-cost path according to the metric used for path computation. Finding one does not itself reroute the label-switched path. The head-end receives a notification and decides whether to perform a graceful reoptimization, such as make-before-break.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting router can ask for a route check, or an intermediate router can check on its own. Finding a better route only sends a notice; the starting router chooses whether to move the traffic.

sections.title: The Signaling Changes
sections.content:
The Path Re-evaluation Request is a new flag in the RSVP SESSION-ATTRIBUTE object. Its value is 0x20. It asks for a check of the current path; it does not request an immediate reroute.

Three new sub-codes for RSVP PathErr Notify error code 25 report that a preferable path exists, local link maintenance is required, or local node maintenance is required. A midpoint may cache a newly computed route briefly; the RFC suggests a default cache time of 5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: A flag asks routers to check for a better route. Notifications distinguish a lower-cost route from planned link or router maintenance, so the head-end can respond appropriately.

sections.title: Triggers, Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
Re-evaluation may be timer-based, event-driven, or operator-driven. Implementations may apply local policies, including rate limits. The procedures are optional: routers that do not recognize the flag must forward it unmodified, and a head-end that does not recognize the new notification sub-codes silently ignores them.

For paths crossing administrative domains, a boundary router may alter a PathErr message to protect confidentiality. A head-end may ignore notifications from another domain. The RFC assigns the new sub-codes under RSVP Notify error code 25.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can choose when route checks happen and limit how often they occur. Routers without the extensions can coexist with supporting routers, and domain boundaries can hide internal details.
